title: Lynx Tech - BCDR playbook & SLA runbook review

Customer to provide ingress network diagram and hosted region constraints (by 2025-11-18)
Schedule a focused runbook tabletop for RTO/RPO on 2025-11-20
action_items: Jordan Fields: Upload SOC2 binder, KMS architecture doc, and runbook links to shared folder by 2025-11-14

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-12
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Fields (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (Lynx CISO), Tom Becker (Lynx Head of Infra), Priya Singh (Lynx Compliance), Miguel Alvarez (Lynx SRE)

Auto-generated summary (optional):
Quick review of Redwood's incident response and BCDR playbooks, alignment on RTO/RPO targets, discussion of SLA uptime guarantees and escalation tiers. Covered SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO behavior, audit log retention and encryption/KMS custody. Agreed next steps to share docs and run a tabletop.

00:00:03 Jordan Fields: Hey everyone, um thanks for joining, I think we have everything queued up. Hi Aisha, can you confirm we good to record?
00:00:10 Aisha Rahman: Yes that's fine, thanks Jordan.
00:00:15 Maya Chen: Cool. I'm Maya SE on the Redwood side, I'll run through the technical pieces and the runbook after Jordan walks through the high level.
00:00:22 Tom Becker: Thanks. We're mainly here to validate RTO/RPO and understand your escalation process — who calls who and SLAs. Also want to make sure KMS model works for our compliance team.
00:00:35 Jordan Fields: Absolutely. Quick agenda: SOC2/ISO artifacts, RBAC/SSO and SCIM provisioning, audit logs and retention, encryption and KMS (custody options), then incident response & BCDR specifics — RTOs/RPOs, runbook steps and who our on-call contacts would be, and finally SLA uptime and escalation flow.
00:00:49 Miguel Alvarez: Can we surface any existing customer playbook examples? Not PII of course, but structure.
00:00:55 Jordan Fields: Yes, we'll share an anonymized playbook — it's in the drive link I'll drop after.

00:01:20 Maya Chen: Jumping into SOC2 and ISO. We have a SOC2 Type II report from 2025 Q2, plus an ISO 27001 certificate for our control environment. I'll just say upfront: the report includes user management, network segmentation, encryption at rest and transit, and incident response control objectives.
00:01:40 Priya Singh: On the ISO side, do you have the Statement of Applicability or the risk assessment outputs?
00:01:46 Maya Chen: We can supply a SoA redacted for customer consumption. The risk assessment output is higher level, but we have control mappings that map to SOC2/ISO and can show how incident response maps to control families.
00:02:02 Aisha Rahman: Okay, that's helpful. Our compliance team will want to map that to our internal controls — thanks.

00:03:00 Tom Becker: On RBAC and SSO — we use Okta and SCIM for provisioning. How granular are your admin roles? We need separation of duties between infra ops and security ops.
00:03:10 Liam Ortiz: Good question. Our RBAC model supports built-in roles: Viewer, Operator, Admin, SecurityAdmin. We also support custom roles with attribute-based scoping; for Okta we support SAML 2.0 and SCIM for automated provisioning. There are a few gotchas — like service-level invite flows for private deployments vs hosted.
00:03:34 Miguel Alvarez: Gotchas?
00:03:36 Liam Ortiz: Yeah — for example, in a private VPC install our SCIM endpoint will be different and provisioning flows may require a short-lived token, so provisioning automation needs a tiny bit of extra orchestration. We'll document in the SCIM/SSO note.
00:03:49 Priya Singh: We also need audit trails when roles are changed — immutable logs for admin role changes for at least 7 years.
00:03:57 Maya Chen: Our audit logs include admin role changes, with actor, timestamp, and source IP. For hosted customers we retain full admin audit for 12 months by default and can extend retention as an add-on; for private deployments we can ship logs to your SIEM and then retention is managed by you. We'll note retention windows in the SOC2 docs.

00:04:35 Aisha Rahman: KMS — we need customer-managed keys (CMK) or HSM-backed keys for at-rest encryption. How do you handle key custody?
00:04:44 Maya Chen: Two options. Hosted: bring-your-own-key (BYOK) via our KMS integration (we support AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, and external HSM via partner connectors). You maintain key rotation and we use envelope encryption where only ciphertext is stored. Private: you can hold keys entirely on-prem or in your cloud account; Redwood can be configured to not have access to plaintext keys. We'll provide the architecture diagram in the artifacts.
00:05:08 Tom Becker: And for backups? We need assurance that backups are encrypted with the same key hierarchy and that restore processes honor key revocation.
00:05:16 Maya Chen: Backups are encrypted and tied to the configured KMS. For BYOK, if a key is revoked we will not be able to restore past snapshots unless you re-provision keys or authorize a key import; that's part of the runbook we walk through for disaster recovery.

00:06:05 Jordan Fields: Jump to incident response and BCDR. Maya will walk through typical incident tiers, RTO/RPO expectations, and our escalation ladder.
00:06:12 Maya Chen: We split incidents into Sev 1 (complete service outage or data-loss event), Sev 2 (partial degradation or significant impact), Sev 3 (minor impact). For our Dedicated customers we publish SLAs per model and per cluster class; typical RTO for a Sev 1 is 30-60 minutes for failover automation, RPO is usually under 5 minutes if KV cache persistence is enabled. For hosted multi-tenant customers RTO can vary — we provide documented fallbacks and degraded mode.
00:06:46 Tom Becker: Wait, RPO under 5 minutes — is that guaranteed? We need contractual numbers for the Dedicated offering.
00:06:52 Jordan Fields: For Dedicated capacity with reserved clusters and KV cache persistence turned on, we can commit to RPO sub-5 minutes in most topologies — we'll put exact numbers and exceptions in the contract addendum. Our SLA defines restoration steps, but the BCDR appendix enumerates those tech pre-reqs.
00:07:09 Miguel Alvarez: And what about cross-region failover? We have a strict data residency requirement for EU-only data.
00:07:16 Maya Chen: For data residency you'd pin to region and we configure routing policies accordingly. Cross-region failover can be disabled for accounts that require strict residency; in that case RTO will be within-region restore rather than cross-region failover. We'll capture that in the runbook and the contract.

00:07:50 Priya Singh: Can you walk us through an incident timeline example for a Sev 1 — who gets paged, and what are expected response SLAs?
00:07:57 Maya Chen: Sure. Example timeline: detection via monitoring at T+0; automated mitigation attempts (circuit breakers, autoscale) T+1-3 minutes; if unresolved, SRE on-call is paged T+3; initial on-call ack within 5 minutes, escalation to SE/lead within 15 minutes; customer-facing communications (status page update and bridge link) within 20 minutes. If service not restored within 30 minutes, exec escalation begins and mitigation runbook (failover or restore) is triggered.
00:08:26 Aisha Rahman: Who is listed as the exec escalation contact? We want a named role and an escalation matrix.
00:08:31 Jordan Fields: We have a tiered matrix: L1 on-call SRE, L2 Redwood SE/infra lead, L3 product ops and customer success, and L4 execs. We'll share the full matrix — it includes phone/Slack/pager contacts. For enterprise customers we can replace contacts with customer-designated counterparts for a joint-run escalation flow.

00:09:10 Tom Becker: Does the SLA include uptime % and credits? We will need clear numbers to align with our procurement.
00:09:15 Jordan Fields: Yes. Our Dedicated SLA tier for production clusters is 99.95% monthly uptime with credits on a sliding scale; for certain configs we can go higher with an enterprise SLA. We'll drop the SLA table in the contract bundle.
00:09:29 Miguel Alvarez: Audit logging granularity — do you capture request-level logs for inference calls for forensic work? How long do you keep them? That's sensitive data.
00:09:39 Maya Chen: For inference call logs we capture metadata (request id, model version, latency, token counts) and optionally the prompt/response payloads if the customer turns on full request logging. For hosted customers we redact PII by default in stored payloads; for private deployments you control retention. Retention windows: metadata 13 months by default, payloads per-customer configurable and typically limited to 90 days unless specified.
00:10:10 Priya Singh: That 90 days is too short for our compliance; we need 7 years for certain logs.
00:10:15 Maya Chen: For enterprise agreements we can extend payload retention by exporting to your long-term storage or streaming to your SIEM (S3/Cloud Storage bucket) where you manage retention to 7 years. We'll include the export pattern in the playbook.

00:11:00 Aisha Rahman: For ransomware-style incidents what is Redwood's role in containment vs customer responsibility?
00:11:08 Jordan Fields: Generally, Redwood contains service-side faults and isolates platform-level issues. If the incident originates from customer-controlled credentials or customer-managed infrastructure (private VPC), containment is handled jointly and customer owns the investigation of their own data plane; we help with artifacts and timelines. We'll define those boundaries in the incident response SLAs.

00:11:40 Tom Becker: Regarding log integrity — is there WORM or tamper-evidence for audit logs?
00:11:46 Maya Chen: We support immutability flags when exporting logs to object storage (WORM on S3) and can sign logs with a rotation key for tamper-evidence. For hosted logs retained by Redwood we maintain an append-only pattern and will provide signed attestations on request.

00:12:30 Miguel Alvarez: I have a technical question about failover: do you use automated leader election and state replication, or is your failover reliant on snapshot restore?
00:12:38 Maya Chen: It's hybrid. For stateful components we use continuous replication for KV where possible; leader election handles the control plane. For larger model caches we rely on cold-start snapshot restore unless persistence is enabled. We'll provide a topology diagram showing which components are replicated versus restored.

00:13:20 Priya Singh: Can you confirm who holds logs for authentication events? For audits we need principal, timestamp, action, success/failure and originating IP.
00:13:29 Liam Ortiz: Yes — auth events are captured with those fields. For SSO via Okta we mirror the SAML assertion ID and correlate it with SCIM provisioning events. We'll provide schema in the audit-log spec doc.

00:14:05 Aisha Rahman: What about legal hold? If we need to preserve data for e-discovery for a litigation hold how do you handle snapshot preservation and export?
00:14:14 Jordan Fields: We support legal hold by creating preserved snapshots and exporting them to your isolated bucket; we can also provide chain-of-custody metadata. There are fees for long-term cold storage but it's supported.

00:15:00 Tom Becker: Let's talk SLA exceptions — what are force majeure and customer-induced outages?
00:15:06 Jordan Fields: Standard exceptions: third-party infra failures (cloud provider outages), customer-managed network misconfigurations, and cases where customer disables replication or key revocation blocks restore. Those are spelled out in the SLA annex.

00:15:40 Miguel Alvarez: For tabletop exercises — we want to simulate a data-plane incident where encryption keys are accidentally rotated. How would the playbook look?
00:15:48 Maya Chen: The tabletop would begin with detection, confirm key rotation cause (human error vs automation), check backup key escrow, attempt key re-import, attempt data restore in isolated environment, and if recovery fails escalate to legal/comms. We'll run a 2-hour workshop to practice. We'll schedule with your DR team.

00:16:30 Priya Singh: Can we set the expected RTO at contract to 2 hours for a critical service? Our business requires that.
00:16:36 Jordan Fields: For Dedicated with cross-region replication and active-active we can discuss a contractual RTO of 2 hours for critical services — it requires specific topology and commit levels; it's doable as an enterprise addendum. We'll model the pricing impact.

00:17:15 Aisha Rahman: Are there any monitoring hooks we need to expose so our tooling can detect pre-failure conditions?
00:17:20 Liam Ortiz: We expose metrics via Prometheus-compatible endpoints for Dedicated/private installs and we can push alerts to your PagerDuty. For hosted we provide webhooks and metric ingest to Datadog or an export to your SIEM.

00:18:00 Tom Becker: About the escalation flow — do you allow a joint war room with our SREs during major incidents?
00:18:06 Jordan Fields: Yes, joint war rooms are standard for enterprise customers; we provision a shared Slack channel or bridge with role-based access and designate L2 contacts who can liaise with your SREs. We'll also offer a runbook to manage communications.

00:18:40 Priya Singh: Regarding evidence for audits: will Redwood sign an SSAE engagement or provide SOC2 subservice org carve-out language?
00:18:49 Maya Chen: We provide SOC2 attestation and then a carve-out letter for subservice where appropriate. For very regulated customers we can also enable control evidence exports for your auditors. We'll include the procedure for auditor access.

00:19:30 Miguel Alvarez: A bit of nitty-gritty: token revocation flows for SSO sessions — how are long-lived sessions handled during an incident?
00:19:38 Liam Ortiz: We issue short-lived tokens by default for API access and support revocation lists for session tokens; during incidents we can invalidate refresh tokens to force re-auth. For delegated service tokens we have an emergency revoke API.

00:20:10 Tom Becker: Let's put some numbers in the runbook example: if detection at 0, failover automation triggers at 2 minutes, human ack at 5 minutes, full failover complete at 45 minutes in the typical case. We need to see median/95th percentiles.
00:20:21 Maya Chen: We'll share SLA telemetry — typical median failover for Dedicated is 12 minutes, 95th at 50 minutes depending on model size and persistence choices. We'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet.

00:21:10 Aisha Rahman: For breach notifications — what is your timeline to notify customers if Redwood identifies a data exfil event?
00:21:17 Jordan Fields: We have a 72-hour notification commitment for confirmed breaches impacting customer data, with preliminary notification within 12 hours if impact is suspected. Notification processes are spelled out in the incident response policy.

00:21:50 Priya Singh: Will that notification include forensic artifacts?
00:21:54 Maya Chen: Yes, we provide an artifacts bundle: logs, timelines, snapshots, and list of affected accounts. Some artifacts may be redacted for privacy but we provide the necessary evidence for incident response.

00:22:30 Miguel Alvarez: Do you have a runbook template we can review before the tabletop?
00:22:36 Jordan Fields: Yes — we'll put the template in the shared drive. It includes roles, checklists, escalation matrix, contact list, and postmortem template.

00:23:10 Tom Becker: On the data residency note again — if we need EU-only, can you guarantee no replication outside EU IP ranges?
00:23:17 Maya Chen: Yes — for EU-only tenants we restrict routing and storage to EU regions and disable cross-region replication. We'll note the controls in the contract.

00:23:45 Priya Singh: A quick question on historical access: who can request a snapshot restore for an archive? Is it the customer only or can Redwood initiate?
00:23:53 Jordan Fields: By default only authorized customer principals can request restores; Redwood can perform restores if authorized in the SOW or during incident response coordination. We'll include approval flows.

00:24:30 Miguel Alvarez: For platform maintenance windows, do you provide advanced notice and scheduled maintenance windows that won't count against SLA?
00:24:36 Liam Ortiz: Yes maintenance windows are scheduled, typically off-peak, with 72-hour notice for non-emergency maintenance. Maintenance-caused downtime is excluded from SLA credits. Emergency maintenance is communicated ASAP and may be excluded as well depending on impact.

00:25:15 Aisha Rahman: Are there post-incident reports and timelines?
00:25:20 Jordan Fields: We provide post-incident reports within five business days for Sev1, including root cause, mitigation steps, and preventive actions.

00:25:50 Tom Becker: Help me understand the difference operationally between Hosted with BYOK and Private with customer-held keys — who is responsible for key lifecycle?
00:25:59 Maya Chen: Hosted BYOK: you manage the key in your cloud KMS and grant Redwood limited permissions; we never store plaintext. Private: keys remain in your environment; Redwood services call your KMS over the private network. Key rotation is customer-managed in both models; we support automation but authority remains with you.

00:26:40 Priya Singh: For the tabletop exercise, can we also test delayed restore where the key is unavailable for 24 hours to simulate legal hold?
00:26:47 Maya Chen: Yes, we can simulate key unavailability and rehearse re-import or recovery steps; we'll script that into the tabletop.

00:27:20 Miguel Alvarez: A question about runbook ownership — is Redwood going to maintain the runbook or will that be joint?
00:27:26 Jordan Fields: Joint ownership is recommended — Redwood maintains the platform-side runbook and we'll work with your team to add customer-specific steps (contacts, network diagrams, credentials). We version the runbook and provide change logs.

00:28:05 Tom Becker: Are we able to lock down admin-initiated restore operations behind multi-party approval?
00:28:11 Liam Ortiz: Yes, we support an approval workflow where two or more principals must approve high-risk operations. We can integrate that with your approval tooling.

00:28:45 Priya Singh: For compliance reporting, will we get periodic attestation or just ad-hoc?
00:28:50 Jordan Fields: Quarterly attestation summary for enterprise customers and ad-hoc evidence exports for audits.

00:29:20 Maya Chen: I'm going to read a short example of the BCDR steps for a Sev1 data-plane incident — expect some stutter in speech.
00:29:28 Maya Chen: (clears throat) Step 1: Detection and validation, gather diagnostics and open an incident ticket. Step 2: Triage, attempt automated mitigations and circuit breakers. Step 3: If unsuccessful, initiate failover to warm standby cluster or restore from snapshot; if KMS key issues, attempt key re-import or use escrowed key procedure. Step 4: Notify customer and open joint war room. Step 5: Execute mitigation and monitor until service restoration. Step 6: Post-incident review and update runbook.
00:30:12 Aisha Rahman: That escrowed key procedure — is that a service you offer?
00:30:18 Maya Chen: We offer a managed escrow service in the enterprise package where rotated keys are vaulted and can be retrieved under strict controls — it's a paid add-on.

00:30:50 Tom Becker: Let's talk about metrics we will track as part of SLA compliance: MTTR, MTTD, RTO, RPO, and availability. Can you supply historical values?
00:30:59 Jordan Fields: Yes we'll provide anonymized historical SLA telemetry for the last 12 months for similar topology customers.

00:31:30 Miguel Alvarez: Any known limitations for large model state transfers?
00:31:35 Maya Chen: Large model caches (multi-GB) can lengthen failover times; when persistence is off cold restarts take longer. We recommend model quantization and warmed pools for critical services; Redwood Optimize has guidance on this.

00:32:10 Priya Singh: On the contractual side, if we accept a 99.95% SLA what are the credit thresholds?
00:32:16 Jordan Fields: Example: <99.95% but >=99.9% yields 10% credit, <99.9% but >=99.0% yields 25% credit, <99.0% yields higher escalated credits. We'll attach the exact table.

00:33:00 Tom Becker: For legal purposes, is Redwood willing to accept indemnity for data breaches caused by platform negligence?
00:33:08 Jordan Fields: Our liability and indemnity are standard for SaaS enterprise deals; we can discuss specific wording with legal, but we typically don't accept unlimited liability. We'll have our legal team follow up.

00:33:45 Maya Chen: Quick note on telemetry hooks — we can stream system health metrics and per-model latency percentiles. For BCDR, we recommend synthetic probes to detect model degradation earlier.

00:34:20 Aisha Rahman: Demo point — can you show the incident timeline in the console?
00:34:25 Maya Chen: I can share a screenshot in the follow-up, but demoing the live console is probably a separate session. We'll schedule a quick walkthrough.

00:34:50 Miguel Alvarez: Any specific customer obligations for patch windows?
00:34:55 Liam Ortiz: Customers should approve maintenance windows and ensure that custom network changes (like firewall rules) are coordinated. We also require admin approvals for major platform changes.

00:35:30 Priya Singh: How are escalations handled outside business hours?
00:35:36 Jordan Fields: 24/7 on-call for Sev1 incidents; on-call routing to Redwood SRE with pager escalation. For lower sevs we have business-hours coverage.

00:36:10 Tom Becker: Do you support contractual testing of DR every 6 months?
00:36:16 Jordan Fields: Yes, we can include biannual DR tests in the SOW for Dedicated and Private customers. We'll capture scheduling and costs.

00:36:50 Maya Chen: One more operational detail: in a mixed deployment where some components are hosted and some are private, we provide a hybrid runbook that delineates responsibilities and handoffs. That often confuses customers, so we make it explicit.

00:37:20 Miguel Alvarez: For ephemeral keys used by runtime — do those rotate automatically?
00:37:25 Liam Ortiz: Yes ephemeral tokens for runtime access rotate frequently; they are short-lived and derived from the primary key via an internal KDF.

00:38:00 Priya Singh: Let's clarify the notification templates for incidents — will those be customer-branded?
00:38:06 Jordan Fields: Yes we support customer-branded incident communications and will white-label status pages for enterprise customers.

00:38:40 Tom Becker: Are there any post-incident compliance attestations you provide?
00:38:45 Maya Chen: Post-incident we provide an attestation letter summarizing the incident and remediation steps for auditors if requested.

00:39:15 Aisha Rahman: I want to be sure our internal legal sees the breach notification SLA and the indemnity wording; please put that in the contract redlines.
00:39:22 Jordan Fields: Will do. We'll have legal follow up with draft language.

00:39:50 Miguel Alvarez: On evidence export — can you stream logs to our SIEM in near-real-time?
00:39:56 Liam Ortiz: Yes we have real-time streaming options to S3, Pub/Sub, or direct SIEM connectors with configurable batching to avoid impacting latency.

00:40:30 Priya Singh: Can we enforce MFA for all admin operations?
00:40:35 Maya Chen: Yes, MFA enforcement is a configurable policy; for higher-risk ops like key export and restores we require MFA + 2-person approval.

00:41:05 Tom Becker: Any final notes about billing impacts for high-availability add-ons?
00:41:11 Jordan Fields: High-availability, cross-region replication, and managed escrow are all priced as add-ons. We'll provide a cost model in the follow-up.

00:41:50 Aisha Rahman: This has been helpful. Let's recap next steps.
00:41:56 Jordan Fields: Recap: Redwood will share SOC2/ISO artifacts, runbook template, SCIM/SSO config note, KMS architecture diagram, and SLA table by 2025-11-14. Lynx to share data residency policy and network diagram by 2025-11-18. Schedule tabletop for 2025-11-20.
00:42:16 Priya Singh: Agreed.
00:42:20 Tom Becker: We'll review and get back on contract addendum items.

00:42:35 Miguel Alvarez: One small question — are there any limitations to forensic exports based on model size?
00:42:41 Maya Chen: Very large payload exports may require staged export and will take longer; we'll include estimated timelines in the artifact.

00:43:10 Aisha Rahman: Any final questions from the Redwood side?
00:43:15 Liam Ortiz: No, thanks.
00:43:18 Jordan Fields: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the link to artifacts and schedule.
00:43:24 (meeting ends)

Auto-generated action items (end):
- Jordan Fields to share SOC2 and SoA redacted materials and KMS diagram.
- Maya Chen to prepare RBAC/SCIM note and runbook template.
- Priya Singh to provide data residency policy and retention windows.

Notes: some transcription artifacts present; occasional speaker overlap and mis-heard words.
